units.source: Whereas some applications use file names to uniquely identify notes, Trilium uses the concept of Note ID.
Generally, the Note ID is a 12-character long alphanumeric sequence (including both lower and upper case letter) that is randomly generated for each new note.
How does the import/export affect the note IDs__TRILIUM_PH_0__
units.context: Note ID > How does the import/export affect the note IDs

units.source: When notes are exported, their note ID is kept in the metadata of the export. However when they are imported back in, a new note ID is generated for all the notes. This also includes other entities that are part of the import/export process such as __TRILIUM_PH_0__Attachments__TRILIUM_PH_1__.
units.context: Note ID > How does the import/export affect the note IDs

units.source: Since the Note ID is a fixed-width randomly generated number, due to the __TRILIUM_PH_0__pigeonhole principle__TRILIUM_PH_1__, there is a possibility that a newly created note will have the same ID as an existing note.

Since the note ID is alphanumeric and the length is 12 we have __TRILIUM_PH_0__ unique IDs. However since we are generating them randomly, we can use a collision calculator such as the one for __TRILIUM_PH_1__Nano ID__TRILIUM_PH_2__ to determine that we'd need to create 1000 notes per hour every hour for 9 centuries in order to have at least 1% probability of a note collision.

As such, Trilium does not take any explicit action against potential note collisions, similar to other software that makes uses of unique hashes such as __TRILIUM_PH_0__Git__TRILIUM_PH_1__. If one would theoretically occur, what would most likely happen is that the existing note will be replaced by the new one.
